title_en: Russia wants to build a new security framework to end the war. This is why it won’t work
excerpt_en: Vladimir Putin wants to counter NATO with his own security pact, but there are reasons to be sceptical.
body_en: When negotiators from Russia, the United States and Ukraine met in Abu Dhabi recently for peace talks on ending the Ukraine war, the Russians pushed a long-held demand for a new security architecture for Europe. Washington has appeared open to this, with US President Donald Trump touting a “big, beautiful agreement” that “might involve all of Europe”.
While little was revealed about what such a framework would look like specifically, a recent speech by Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov provides some clues.

Sergei Lavrov’s speech at the Minsk International Conference on Eurasian Security. At a security conference in Minsk, Belarus, earlier this month, Lavrov proposed a new security architecture for the entire Eurasian continent.

Reiterating the claim Russia has long made to justify its war in Ukraine, Lavrov said NATO had repeatedly pledged not to expand eastward to contain Russia, but did so anyway. And, he said, the West is now pursuing a new “NATO-style military-political bloc in Asia”.
In response, Lavrov said Russia wanted to build a new security framework that would encompass all of Europe and Asia – echoing the Soviet Union’s communist alliances during the Cold War.

A new arrangement like this would be “committed to the principles of indivisible security, openness and equality”, Lavrov said, adding European nations were welcome to join. Russia does not “desire nor plan any war whatsoever with Europe”, he stressed. But he added:
If Europe, as it threatens, is itself preparing for war and initiates one, we are ready.
A security proposal based on “sovereignty” and “equality” may sound appealing to some states across the region. However, there are several reasons to be sceptical.

What Europe wants The prevailing view in Europe is that Russia is the continent’s principal security threat. So, the idea of European states joining Russia in a new arrangement of any sort is unlikely to gain broad acceptance.

And despite Russian President Vladimir Putin’s claims he is not against “ having a dialogue with Europe, Moscow has made clear it does not want European representatives in the Ukraine peace talks. So it stands to reason Europe wouldn’t have a voice in a future security agreement either.

That said, the political view towards Russia in Europe is evolving. As economic pressures continue to mount, support for right-wing, populist parties is growing, including one of Ukraine’s staunchest supporters, Germany.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party opposes financial and military support for Ukraine, arguing the war is not in Germany’s national interests.
In fact, its platform in one recent eastern state election where it finished first called for a revival of Russian language teaching, an end to sanctions and closer energy ties with Russia.
This highlights the diversity of views in some countries on both the war and Europe’s broader strategic priorities.

Some have raised the possibility of a more robust Organization for Security and Co-operation (the only European security group that Russia belongs to), or a revived NATO-Russia Council. However, this seems far-fetched in the absence of trust between the two sides.
Many in Europe believe Russia’s true aims for a new security framework are to carve up the continent into Cold War-era spheres of influence and expand its influence beyond its borders.
Read more: Russia wanted a new world order. This wasn’t the one it had in mind
What China wants Second, it remains unclear how China, the region’s other major power, and its own security ambitions fit within Russia’s vision.

Chinese foreign policy has long emphasised a principle of not interfering in the domestic affairs of other states. This has proven attractive to many authoritarian countries. At the same time, China has successfully advanced major global economic initiatives, notably the Belt and Road Initiative. And Beijing often promotes its own vision of the international order.
As such, Russia’s proposed security framework would need to accommodate another major power with its own interests and priorities.

Despite their growing cooperation in recent years, China and Russia are also competing for influence in a pivotal Eurasian region – Central Asia. While Russia has traditionally been the dominant power in the region, China has quietly advanced to the point where it can now compete with, if not surpass, Russia’s influence.

What the rest of Asia wants Lastly, Eurasia is already home to a complex landscape of international organisations, blocs and multilateral security agreements. Beyond the European Union, these include the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, the BRICS (the group originally comprised of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa), and the Gulf Cooperation Council, among others.

title_en: Elon Musk has approval to launch 1 million satellites. An astronomer explains how this would impact the sky
excerpt_en: If Starmind proceeds in full, the number of operational satellites will be multiplied by a factor of 50.
body_en: A long-exposure image of the Orion Nebula with a total exposure time of 208 minutes showing satellite trails in mid-December 2019. A. H. Abolfath/Wikimedia This week, on the eve the Thanksgiving holiday, the United States Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s plan to launch one million “ Starmind ” artificial intelligence (AI) data centre satellites. This decision reflects the convergence of a satellite boom, an AI bubble and the Trump administration’s disregard for environmental regulation.
If Starmind proceeds in full, the number of operational satellites will be multiplied by a factor of 50. Space and our night skies will become vastly busier places.
SpaceX’s pitch is to take the impact of data centres away from Earth, using a million solar-powered satellites to do AI data crunching in space and beam the results to Earth.
But what is the impact of one million satellites, both in space and on Earth? Why has the Federal Communications Commission made this decision? And will a million satellites actually end up in orbit?
Ups and downs We are currently in a satellite boom, and constellations of hundreds or thousands of satellites are a key feature.

The Starlink internet satellites (another SpaceX project) is the best known example of such a constellation. Orbital rocket launches have increased to almost one per day, while the number of operational satellites is creeping towards 20,000.
But Starmind represents something else. A million satellites.

To get so many satellites into orbit would be a vast undertaking. If the satellites have a lifetime of five years (similar to Starlink satellites), then roughly 500 satellites would need to be launched every day.

This also implies that roughly 500 satellites would eventually need to be disposed of every day. For satellites less than 2,000 kilometres above Earth, disposal usually means reentry and burning up in the atmosphere. And this has consequences.

When satellites burn up in the atmosphere, their materials react with and are deposited into the upper atmosphere. We now have satellites depositing far more aluminium, titanium, copper and lead into the atmosphere than the natural quantities from meteors.
Aluminium is of particular concern, as alumina can lead to the destruction of ozone in the upper atmosphere. This could increase ultraviolet light on Earth and the risk of skin cancers.
It’s getting busy Increasing the number of satellites by a factor of 50 is going to change our view of the sky.
If you look up during the early evening, you will see the stars your ancestors saw. But within a minute or two you will see a satellite. A point of light silently moving from horizon to horizon.
Satellites are already common enough, and Starmind would make matters worse. Our view of the night skies could fundamentally change.

Each satellite would be 75 metres wide and in the early evening they will be brighter than any star. And with a million satellites in orbit, there will be hundreds of Starmind satellites above the horizon irrespective of where you are.
The orbital clutter comes with real risks.

Satellites travel at speeds of roughly seven kilometres per second, and collisions produce clouds of debris that can produce further collisions. A nightmare scenario is the Kessler Syndrome – a runaway cascade of debris producing collisions that render low Earth orbit unusable.

Of course, SpaceX is aware of the risks of orbital collisions, and it already mitigates this risk with Starlink by manoeuvring satellites away from potential collisions. However, such manoeuvres require operational satellites and it is inevitable some satellites will fail.
Those uncontrolled satellites will pose a real danger.

Regulator or promoter? The Federal Communications Commission has been a key regulator for American satellites. This has included regulating the radio frequencies that satellites use for communications to and from Earth, the disposal of satellites at the end of their useful lives and environmental impacts.

However, under the Trump administration, the commission is taking a looser approach to regulating satellites. This includes no consideration of environmental impacts, which is reflected in the commission’s decision on Starmind. It says the commission “will not require further environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act […] for SpaceX’s Starmind system”.

There are also some statements from the commission on Starmind that are, quite frankly, bizarre. For example, it claims Starmind “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”.

title_en: Trump Urges Putin to ‘Pull Back’ Military Aggression in Europe
excerpt_en: The U.S. President expressed hope that a deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine "quickly" to avoid expansion of the war.

title_en: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv launched more long-range strikes in 2026 than rest of war combined, data shows
excerpt_en: Ukrainian strikes on targets more than 500km away increased, with Siberia and Libya among the locations hit. What we know on day 1,738
body_en: Ukraine launched nearly 500 strikes at Russian targets more than 500km away in 2026 – more than in the first four years of the war combined, according to data from the ACLED conflict monitor. Most of the attacks hit Russian territory, with Ukrainian drones reaching Moscow, St Petersburg and as far away as Siberia, and AFP analysis of ACLED’s figures up to 20 November showed. Some targets were as far as 1,500km away from both sides, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claiming strikes on two vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday that sank a Russian warship. As early as December 2025, ACLED recorded a strike by Kyiv in the Mediterranean, near the Greek and Libyan coasts, on an oil tanker from Russia’s “shadow fleet”. It said the incident was considered the first attack of its kind in the area since the start of the war.

Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha expressed “regret” over the “unintended consequences” of a Ukrainian attack on Russian ships in the Libyan port of Benghazi, saying it was directed at Moscow, not at Libya. After speaking ⁠to his Libyan counterpart, Sybiha, writing on X, said Ukraine had no intention of extending the war against Russia to Libya or ⁠any other country. Ukraine says it sank the Russian naval corvette and a cargo ship on Sunday because they were transporting military equipment. But the attack, which killed two ⁠Libyan army personnel, was condemned by Libya’s western-backed government of national unity based in Tripoli, and by the eastern-based ‌Libyan National ‌Army (LNA) General Command, which has ties with Russia.

US President Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Vladimir Putin to “pull back all military aggression” against Europe, in another shift in tone towards the Russian leader. Trump said he thought it would help lead to a deal to end the war in Ukraine. The statement – which did not specify which territories Trump meant and did not specifically include Ukraine – comes a day after Trump hosted Nato chief Mark Rutte in Florida, where the two leaders called on Russia not to expand the Ukraine war. “During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe,” Trump said on his Truth Social network.

Zelenskyy on Thursday said Ukraine had information that Russia was planning a ⁠big attack on ⁠the country in the coming days. “Unfortunately, we have information about a new mass ⁠strike being prepared by the Russians,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address. “In the coming ⁠days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats. And in Russia, ‌they should know ‌that we will rebuild what is ours and retaliate ‌against every Russian strike.” The warning was the second issued by the president this week.

Ukrainian military intelligence said Ukrainian drones had struck an oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar ⁠region, and oil reservoirs at Russia’s Transneft oil facility in the central Bashkortostan region overnight. The Marinovka military ‌airfield in the Volgograd region was hit also. A drone attack claimed by Ukraine on Thursday set a major Russian refinery on fire and caused serious damage, the owner said, weeks after a previous strike forced a halt to its production.

EU leaders were bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year. Arriving in Brussels on Thursday, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, reiterated his view that all EU member states should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. “When the European Union provides funding, it does so as the European Union – and that union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24,” he said. Merz has previously threatened to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget unless all countries sign up to the Ukraine loan.

title_en: Water firms to identify 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts
excerpt_en: Department for Work and Pensions to provide data about households missing out on WaterSure support scheme
body_en: Water companies will use government data to identify as many as 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts, after criticism that not enough people are aware of the £428 support for their annual bills.

The Department for Work and Pensions will provide information to identify and contact a quarter of a million households who are missing out on support to which they are entitled under the WaterSure scheme.
The scheme is open to people on benefits who need to use a lot of water either for medical reasons or because their household has three or more children under 19.

The government said that 300,000 customers are signed up to WaterSure, but fewer than half of eligible households claim it because either they are unaware or they may have difficulty proving they qualify.

The Labour government has sought to portray itself as tough on the water industry. However, Andy Burnham has yet to outline his plan for the sector, despite saying he would bring in “more public control” of companies.
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said it was “common sense” to share information about eligible households with companies.

“Hundreds of thousands of the most vulnerable people aren’t getting help with their water bills because they don’t know how to access it,” she said. “That’s not right. By sharing data across government and water companies, we’re fixing that problem – meaning getting that help will be far easier for those who need it.”
The changes received the backing of Martin Lewis, founder of the MoneySavingExpert advice website.

He said: “Too many people miss out on help they desperately need and are entitled to. Water companies shoulder some blame for confusing applications and underpublicising support. Yet it is important the government joins the dots too. If one part of the state knows someone needs help, another shouldn’t leave them in the dark. Help is only effective if it actually reaches those who need it.”

Eagle also announced that the Consumer Council for Water, which helps households with complaints, will be given new powers to investigate water companies’ customer service and work with regulators to rectify problems. It will be named the Water Watchdog.

A spokesperson for Water UK, a lobby group for the industry, said: “Water companies have long called for government to automatically provide us with the information needed to give people heavily discounted water bills. As a result, hundreds of thousands more people will now benefit from WaterSure.”

title_en: Southern and central Australia face summer of heightened bushfire risk and heatwaves
excerpt_en: Fire chiefs say large swathes of the country are at risk from fires driven by high fuel loads, dry soil and hot weather
body_en: Large parts of southern and central Australia face elevated fire risk this summer, authorities say, while heatwaves and extreme temperatures are likely nationwide.

Most of Victoria, eastern Tasmania and large parts of South Australia, Western Australia, New South Wales and the Northern Territory face heightened bushfire risk – driven by high fuel loads, low soil moisture and forecast hot and dry conditions – according to the seasonal outlook from the Australian and New Zealand Council for Fire and Emergency Services (AFAC), released on Friday.
Related: Flinders Island bushfire: Out-of-control fire with flames 10-metres high destroys at least six homes in Tasmania

The AFAC chief executive, Rob Webb, said nearly every state had areas of above average risk heading into the hottest part of the year. He urged people to make sure they had a plan and to talk to family and neighbours.
“ Know what you’re going to do and know where you’ll get your information – don’t wait till the fire’s there,” he said.

In Victoria, the dire outlook followed back-to-back years of devastating fires and record-breaking heat. Recent rains had spurred abundant grass growth in places, which could dry rapidly, creating the potential for grassfires as the weather warms up, AFAC said.
Last summer, more than 440,000 hectares of land burned across Victoria – an area larger than the Black Saturday fires of 2009. That followed major fires in the Grampians national park in 2024-25.
The state’s emergency management commissioner, Tim Wiebusch, warned that bushfires wouldn’t be the only risk Victorians would have to deal with.

“We’ve also seen in recent times the storm risk here in Victoria. We’ve seen flash flooding, we’ve seen low levels of riverine flooding, but we’ve also seen earthquakes, and we’ve seen the risk of thunderstorm asthma,” he said.
“All Victorians need to prepare for a mixed bag of emergencies over our high-risk weather season as we come through the summer months.”
In Tasmania, residents on Flinders Island were already contending with an out-of-control blaze, after a warm and dry year, and rainfall well below average.

“Tasmania has been particularly dry,” Webb said. “The fuel is there to burn, it’s just a matter of whether we get the weather conditions, the windy conditions, that allow fires to become established.”

Climate councillor Dr Andrew Watkins said a complex combination of factors – including the strong El Niño, a positive Indian Ocean Dipole, and influences from Antarctica – were combining with long-term warming to create tinderbox conditions in parts of the country.

Global heating, fuelled by the burning of fossil fuels, was already having an influence on fires across the world, said Watkins, adjunct professor at Monash University’s School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment.
“South-eastern Australia is one of the most bushfire-prone places in the entire world,” he said.
“Nowhere on that map is low risk. Everyone needs to prepare, and unfortunately climate change is going to mean that’s the norm for the future.”

Hotter than usual days and nights were likely nationwide between December and February, which could lead to extreme temperatures and heatwaves, according to the Bureau of Meteorology. North-western Australia and eastern Tasmania were forecast to be drier than usual in summer, while above average rainfall was expected for Queensland and north-eastern New South Wales. Oceans around Australia were mostly much warmer than usual, with the temperature expected to rise over coming months.
Related: World has six consecutive days 2C above preindustrial levels for first time
In its summer outlook, the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority was forecasting a high risk of widespread coral bleaching, with marine heatwaves up to 2C warmer than average expected.

The Australian Marine Conservation Society has called for an emergency response plan for the reef, which could include temporary protections for critical reefs to restrict certain activities, like removing coral.

“Everyone is very worried,” said Dr Lissa Schindler, the AMCS’s campaign manager. “The Great Barrier Reef is heading into another dangerous summer, with El Niño threatening to intensify marine heatwaves across the whole World Heritage Area.
“The warning lights are flashing red. We need to be throwing everything that we can at this, to give the reef a fighting chance.”

title_en: Can the International Criminal Court survive Trump’s attacks – and hold world leaders to account?
excerpt_en: The trial of former president of the Philippines, Rodrigo Duterte, comes at a precarious moment for the International Criminal Court, as the US ramps up its efforts to undermine the institution.
body_en: More than eight years after Rodrigo Duterte announced the Philippines would withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), the country’s former president is about to begin his trial in The Hague.
Duterte faces charges of crimes against humanity over alleged killings carried out during his deadly war on drugs.
The trial, which begins on 30 November, comes at a precarious moment for the court, as the United States ramps up its efforts to undermine the institution.

“Nothing has really quite approached this level of hostility we’re seeing coming from President Trump, or more particularly Marco Rubio,” explains Carrie McDougall, an associate professor at Melbourne Law School, speaking on The Conversation Weekly podcast.

The US has never joined the ICC, citing concerns about politically motivated prosecutions of its nationals. But the court can investigate alleged war crimes committed by Americans on the territory of its member countries.
McDougall says the US has “made no bones” about its opposition to the investigation of US nationals and the prosecution of Israeli nationals.

In October, the Trump administration extended sanctions against individual ICC judges and prosecutors to the court as a whole. The sanctions threaten the court’s access to banking and IT services, as well as its ability to engage with victims and witnesses, McDougall says.
The US has also been pressuring countries to withdraw from the court. McDougall attributes the decisions by Venezuela, Chad and Nauru to withdraw from the ICC to that pressure.
Meanwhile, Duterte’s case illustrates both the powers and limitations of the court.

“The reality is that the court itself doesn’t have any enforcement powers,” McDougall says. Instead, it relies on the Security Council – which has never used its enforcement powers to assist the court – and countries to cooperate with it.

Duterte was arrested by his own country’s authorities. Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu are both subject to ICC arrest warrants, but Russia and Israel have refused to cooperate in the arrest of their leaders. Neither country is a member of the ICC.

While the ICC doesn’t have its own enforcement powers, arrest warrants still have some power; they can restrict leaders’ ability to travel overseas and potentially deter others from committing crimes. And, McDougall says:
There is no statute of limitations, so those ICC arrest warrants can be enforced after individuals have lost power and lost the protection of their states.
Duterte’s case also demonstrates that withdrawing from the ICC does not necessarily shield political leaders from prosecution, explains McDougall.
Once a state … files a notice of withdrawal, it takes a year to become effective, and the ICC retains jurisdiction over any crimes committed up until that effective withdrawal date.

McDougall says the US sanctions “will impede the court’s ability to fulfil its mandate” and that the threat is “very serious.” She also warns that US attacks on international institutions risk emboldening other countries, including China and Russia, that want to reshape that order.
“I think we are facing something of a crossroads,” she says.
McDougall describes the ICC as the “canary in the coal mine” for the international legal order:

It is required to hold to account those responsible for international crimes, particularly when we’re talking about the leaders of states. And so that puts a really big target on its back for would-be spoilers.
Ultimately, though, McDougall does not expect a mass exodus from the ICC.
I think a lot will actually hinge on how robustly other ICC states’ parties stand up for the court.

Carrie McDougall does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

title_en: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
excerpt_en: Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum
body_en: In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions.

They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets.
Related: After 80 years in Oxford, Naga ancestors are finally going home

Also on display are protective ritual objects, taken by the British from Gaidinliu’s hiding places, which they believed she had used against them. These are a stick with a monkey skull used to ward off evil spirits, and small wooden clubs, traditionally used by Naga people to cast an omen on an enemy.

The exhibition, The Afterlives of Captured Objects, raises questions about the colonial extraction of artefacts from Indigenous communities, which were often originally catalogued using prejudiced and discriminatory language, according to the curator, Clare Harris, a professor of visual anthropology.

For example, Harris said Gaidinliu’s notebooks were derided as “meaningless scribbling” by the colonial anthropologist JP Mills, who collected them. But he also recorded that these writings “gave her immense prestige”, which suggests that they may have been seized as part of British efforts to suppress the religious and political movement that Gaidinliu led, called Heraka.

While most of the objects on display were taken by the British after Gaidinliu abandoned them while on the run, two items were more violently extracted. Textiles displayed on mannequins in the show were taken from a pair of male and female sacred clay figures from a Heraka temple in the village of Kambiron in 1931.
The textiles are shown along with a photograph taken by a British officer of another soldier kneeling with the sacred figures, which were destroyed along with the temple.

“By showing the photograph at the same time, you can make the equation visually about what was extracted by the British there,” said Harris. “The British destroy the temple and they destroy the figures, so they take away the potency of those things.”

The show follows a four-year project by researchers from India and the Universities of Edinburgh and Oxford to digitise the Gaidinliu collection and share it with Naga communities in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. Their craftspeople have used the images to revive and revitalise traditional crafts such as basket weaving and textile making, with some of their creations included in the exhibition.

Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at the school of divinity, University of Edinburgh, who co-led the project with Harris, said attempts were also being made to translate Gaidinliu’s notebooks in an effort to reconstruct a new Indigenous language for the Naga people.
He said: “There are some symbols which are recognisable within stories and myths. They may be untranslatable in a conventional sense but they are being used to try and construct a language system.”

The exhibition also aims to raise international recognition of Gaidinliu, who has long been revered as an important leader in the resistance movement that led to Indian independence. After her release from prison in 1947, she became head of a political movement advocating for recognition of a Naga homeland.

Alila Chang, one of Gaidinliu’s grandnieces, said her family felt a deep sense of pride about the exhibition. She said: “These objects are connected to our family’s history and the struggles and sacrifices of our people as well. We want the world to know her struggles and for what reason she fought.”
Chang, who has come to Oxford for the exhibition’s private view, also shared a more personal recollection of Gaidinliu as a “very affectionate grandmother”.
“I remember [her] giving us sweets,” she said, adding how Gaidinliu, who died in 1993, would pray for her and her sibling when they went to school in the morning.
“She will always be in our hearts, but I think she belongs to the world now.”

title_en: Palantir has created bespoke tech solutions for the NHS | Letter
excerpt_en: Letter: Stephen Childs responds to a letter that said the US software firm was not the right fit for Britain’s health service
body_en: Prof Caroline Mitchell is right that US systems designed for an insurance market are rife in the NHS ( Letters, 18 November). But Palantir’s software isn’t among them – and should not be confused with a range of other systems, some designed as far back as the 1970s for billing and then exported to the NHS over the following decades.

Our story is different. Each application built on the federated data platform – which connects information across the NHS – is bespoke to the NHS and to the healthcare trust that uses it. The NHS is a highly complex, loose association of healthcare trusts and commissioners, with data that is rich, but often unstructured and frustratingly disconnected.

Through the national federated data platform, our software is helping to fix that with a range of tools purpose-built for the NHS, which perform functions like speeding up cancer diagnosis – not one of which has been adopted from the insurance market.

I speak from experience, having worked for the NHS for more than 30 years and having been responsible for building one of these unique applications in partnership with Palantir to tackle delayed discharges.
How data is managed in the NHS is a critical debate. We need to get the facts right or patient care and taxpayer value for money will suffer. Stephen Childs Special adviser, Palantir

title_en: An Alarming Spike in Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Was Hiding in Plain Sight in a Federal Dataset
excerpt_en: The post An Alarming Spike in Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Was Hiding in Plain Sight in a Federal Dataset appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Ectopic pregnancy deaths have nearly doubled in the United States in recent years. Shawn Patrick Ouellette/Portland Portland Press Herald/Getty Images For years, ProPublica has examined maternal health and the ongoing impacts of abortion bans since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Data analysis has been central to that effort, offering a quantitative view into an area that has long been underresearched, especially as studying the impact of abortion bans has become politicized and federal agencies have been gutted under the Trump administration.

For example, last year my colleagues uncovered a dramatic rise in sepsis rates since Texas instituted its abortion ban, which carries the strictest penalties for healthcare providers. The number of blood transfusions during emergency room visits for first-trimester miscarriage spiked in the state as well.

Most recently, my colleagues Andrea Suozzo, Sophie Chou, Kavitha Surana and I examined pregnancy-related deaths on a national level. We turned our attention to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. The agency collects information from death certificates and publishes totals based on variables like location, demographics and cause of death. It’s a commonly used resource for journalists and academics who want to learn more about trends in mortality.

Deaths involving an ectopic pregnancy are presented as a rate within three-year intervals to meet data suppression thresholds. Source: ProPublica analysis of CDC WONDER multiple cause of death and natality data. Lucas Waldron/ProPublica The increase was particularly stark in states that had banned abortion.

Deaths involving an ectopic pregnancy are grouped into three-year periods to meet data suppression thresholds. States with abortion bans that begin at six weeks of pregnancy or earlier are considered to have a strict ban. Source: ProPublica analysis of CDC WONDER multiple cause of death and natality data. Lucas Waldron/ProPublica This was a significant and serious finding. And as far as we could tell, the fact that the number of women who died from ectopic pregnancies nearly doubled after abortion bans came into effect hadn’t been reported before.

A death from an ectopic pregnancy should be a “never event,” according to Dr. Alice Abernathy, an OB-GYN in Philadelphia. And yet, as we later confirmed, more than a dozen leaders in the field of maternal health were unaware of the spike. Neither state governments nor the federal government, whose own dataset we were using, had publicly identified this trend.
How could it be that seemingly no one was aware of this but us?

The answer, as it turns out, is multifold and begins with the nature of the condition itself. Ectopic pregnancies occur when an embryo fails to properly implant in the uterus and begins to develop elsewhere, most commonly inside a fallopian tube. The pregnancy grows until it causes the organ to rupture, triggering catastrophic bleeding.
It is a rare condition, estimated to impact up to 2% of pregnancies, but it is incredibly dangerous.
“I genuinely thought I was going to die,” said Kyleigh Thurman, whose right fallopian tube ruptured after she struggled to get ectopic care in Texas in 2023.

“There were a few times I asked my husband if I was going to die,” Leitaea Lowrimore of Oklahoma said in an ongoing lawsuit challenging an abortion ban, after being denied treatment for an ectopic pregnancy at multiple hospitals in February. “I kept thinking about our kids.”

Even before ectopic pregnancy deaths began rising, the condition was noted as the leading cause of death in the first trimester of pregnancy. Yet it has received little research attention. For example, the CDC doesn’t track how many ectopic pregnancies occur a year and doesn’t require healthcare providers to report them. The most recent nationwide study we could find examined data only through 2013.

The U.S. doesn’t conduct national maternal mortality reviews in the same way as countries like the United Kingdom, which responded to a similar spike in the years after the COVID-19 pandemic by instituting changes to emergency services and promoting awareness of ectopic pregnancy symptoms. Instead, in our country, much of the work of investigating pregnancy-related deaths is left to state committees.

This creates a large potential knowledge gap. In individual states, the number of ectopic deaths is small and subject to a lot of variation, making it harder to spot a trend. After our story was published, we reached out to maternal mortality review committees in states with abortions bans; many of them responded that they didn’t identify an increase in ectopic deaths and that, despite the findings of our reporting, they had no plans to examine this issue further.
We realized the fact that nearly double the number of women are dying from ectopic pregnancies is visible at only the national level.

It is unclear why the CDC and other federal agencies across two administrations have failed to publicly respond to the increase in deaths despite having access to the same information ProPublica analyzed. We reached out to the CDC to ask what the agency has done to investigate or address this trend. It has epidemiologists who review death and birth records and has in the past done its own investigations and analyses. A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, didn’t provide a direct answer to that question but said the agency continues to track maternal mortality trends, investigate their causes and provide funding for research.

Maternal experts agree that the government’s capacity to respond to this trend has been significantly reduced as a result of the staffing cuts initiated by the Trump administration since the beginning of last year. The CDC’s Division of Reproductive Health, for example, lost most of its 100 employees, according to a lawsuit filed by more than a dozen states’ attorneys general last year.
